sentences.text: The largest known specimen of Besanosaurus is estimated to be about 8 meters long.
This animal possessed a long, thin snout containing numerous small, pointed teeth.
The tail of Besanosaurus made up more than half of the animal's total length and had a downward bend.
Besanosaurus had forelimbs longer than its hindlimbs, with round and squat humeri.
The genus Besanosaurus was named by Dal Sasso and Pinna in 1996.
The holotype specimen of Besanosaurus is the nearly complete flattened skeleton designated BES SC 999.
Specimens previously classified as the genus Mikadocephalus have been reinterpreted as belonging to Besanosaurus.
All confirmed specimens of Besanosaurus originate from the Besano Formation.
Researchers suggest Besanosaurus had strong jaw muscles and fed on small fish and coleoid cephalopods using rapid snapping bites.
Besanosaurus likely swam by undulating its body like an eel, suggesting modest speed but capable of rapid acceleration and good maneuverability.
Besanosaurus was a carnivore that primarily ate small fish, cephalopods, and other marine reptiles.
Mikadocephalus gracilirostris is a synonym of Besanosaurus leptorhynchus.
The parent group of Besanosaurus is Besanosauridae.
Bindellini and colleagues concluded in 2024 that there is no evidence of Besanosaurus from Svalbard.
Besanosaurus lived during the Middle Triassic, specifically the latest Anisian stage.
Besanosaurus fossils are found in Monte San Giorgio, a region spanning Italy and Switzerland.
During the Anisian, the Besano Formation represented a lagoon inhabited by diverse marine life including other ichthyosaurs.
Some researchers have debated whether Besanosaurus might actually be another specimen of the genus Shastasaurus.
Sander considered it possible that Wimanius was a juvenile Besanosaurus rather than a distinct genus.
Sander argued that better-preserved material needed to be studied before definite taxonomic assignments could be made.
McGowan and Motani considered both Mikadocephalus and Wimanius potentially synonymous with Pessosaurus, though they remained tentative because the material was not studied firsthand.
Maisch and Matzke noted in 2000 that the fossil material of P. suevicus might come from Besanosaurus but agreed it could not be distinguished from other group representatives.
